clue.text: Train – train endlessly, train endlessly (4-4)

indicators.note: Endlessly means with no ends at all, so the word gives up the letter at each end before anything else happens.

blocks.note: to school someone is to train them, and SCHOOL stripped of its outer S and L leaves these four letters
the same instruction is given a second time, for the same four letters again

explanation.surface: Relentless drilling: the order to train given over and over with no end in sight.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first 'train' is the definition; the other two are the verb, to school. 'Endlessly' taking both ends off a word rather than just the last letter is the step solvers miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A choo-choo is a train in nursery language, the word copied from the noise a steam engine makes.

clue.text: Secures in carriage, sandwiched between twin sons (6)

indicators.note: Something sandwiched between two things has one of them on either side of it, so the carriage takes the middle and the boys the outsides.

blocks.note: s = son, and twins makes two of them, one for each end
a trap is a light two-wheeled carriage pulled by a pony

explanation.surface: Fastening something down inside a carriage, wedged between a pair of twin boys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secures' is the verb, as in strapping a load down. A trap is the small horse-drawn carriage of Victorian streets, a word that survives in Britain in 'pony and trap'.
explanation.definitionFit: To strap a thing is to secure it with a band or belt, so definition and answer are the same verb in the same tense.

clue.text: Once more show up a rep being doubly wrong (8)

indicators.note: Doubly means the thing is done twice over, so the letters to work from are written out a second time before they are touched.
Letters that have come out wrong are not standing in the order they should be, and have to be set right in a different one.

blocks.note: the four letters of A REP taken twice over, eight letters in all

explanation.surface: A sales rep who has been wrong twice over turning up at the door again.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is only four letters long, which is what hides it: 'doubly' has to be read as an instruction to write them out again before rearranging anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To reappear is to come into sight a second time, which is what showing up once more amounts to.

clue.text: Lost opportunity in double withdrawal (4,2)

definitions.note: The surface offers 'lost opportunity' as a noun phrase, but it is doing duty as a past-tense verb and its object — lost the opportunity — which is what the answer means.

indicators.note: What is in something sits inside it, and here the answer sits inside the two words that follow, unbroken.

blocks.note: the letters run straight on through the phrase: douBLE WIThdrawal

explanation.surface: A chance thrown away in the middle of taking money out twice.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden words hide best across a word boundary, and this one straddles one: the gap in the answer falls in a different place from the gap in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To blow it is to squander the chance you were given, so the past tense says a lost opportunity exactly.

clue.text: That island repeatedly disturbed this island (6)

indicators.note: Something disturbed has been knocked out of the arrangement it was in, so its letters have to settle into another one.

blocks.note: the word itself, four of the six letters
i = island in atlases and gazetteers, and 'repeatedly' asks for it twice

explanation.surface: One island shaken again and again by the weather, with another island beside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That' points at nothing — it is four of the six letters as they stand. The doubling that runs through this puzzle is what supplies the second island abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Tahiti is the main island of French Polynesia, so 'this island' points straight at the answer while 'that island' was only a letter.

clue.text: Moreover, encored excessively (3-3)

blocks.note: moreover = too, as in 'and this too'
an encore is the same performance given again, so the same three letters come round once more

explanation.surface: A singer called back for more encores than the evening could bear.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's 'O, that this too too solid flesh would melt' is where this doubled word lives, and it survives as a mannered way of calling something excessive. Shakespeare wrote it without the hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: Too-too means excessively, the affected intensifier that Hamlet's 'too too solid flesh' left behind in the language.

clue.text: Person distributing shares is fraudster if doubly so (6)

definitions.note: The second half does not define the word on its own: it says what the word becomes once 'double-' is put in front of it, which is the puzzle's theme rather than a synonym.

blocks.note: whoever hands out the portions — the cards round a card table, or stock on a trading floor
put 'double-' in front and the honest job becomes the standard name for a cheat

explanation.surface: The man handing out the shares, twice as crooked as he looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shares' pulls towards the stock market, and the word covers the hands dealt at a card table just as well. Only the first half is a definition; the second needs a prefix before it works.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer is whoever hands out the cards or the shares; and a double-dealer, the same word twice over, is a fraudster.

clue.text: Indication of ‘again’ verbally supported by a boy, and why (6)

indicators.note: What is supported by something rests on top of it, so in a down entry the supporting letters go underneath.

blocks.note: re- is the prefix bolted onto a verb to say the action happened again: redo, rerun, rebuild
the article as it stands
a boy of the family is a son

explanation.surface: A spoken hint that something is happening again, propped up by a young lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Verbally' is not the homophone flag it looks like: the prefix wanted is the one that goes on verbs. The definition is the last word of the clue on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: The why of a thing is its reason — 'the whys and wherefores' — so the question word stands in for the noun.

clue.text: Reaffirmed commitment, thus made pillow much softer (7,4)

definitions.note: The second half is not a synonym but a literal reading of the phrase's own words, taking down as the feather filling, which is why 'thus' sits between the two halves.

blocks.note: stuck to a course already chosen, and staked more on it
read the second word as the feathers inside a pillow, and twice as many of them is what softens it

explanation.surface: Someone standing by a promise, and plumping up a pillow while doing it.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from blackjack, where you double your bet and take one more card on it. The second reading takes the feathers literally, which is where the puzzle's theme comes in.
explanation.definitionFit: To double down is to commit harder to a course already taken; read literally, twice the down in a pillow is what makes it softer.

clue.text: Shade in US area, with same again for state (8)

blocks.note: color is the American spelling, and a color is a shade
standard abbreviation
do. is the written abbreviation for ditto, the list-keeper's mark for the same again

explanation.surface: Painting an area of America in a shade, then giving it another coat of the same.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue tells you which side of the Atlantic to spell on: an American state takes the American spelling. 'Do' for ditto is what a clerk writes down a column to save repeating himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Colorado is one of the fifty American states, so 'state' names it by category rather than by synonym.

clue.text: More than once, clumsily handle fruit (6)

blocks.note: to paw something is to handle it roughly and clumsily
the instruction to do it again supplies the same three letters a second time

explanation.surface: A shopper pawing over the fruit on a market stall again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: Doubling a word is this puzzle's whole trick, and here it turns rough handling into something you can eat — the tropical fruit sold in most British shops as papaya.
explanation.definitionFit: The pawpaw is the tropical fruit Britain mostly sells as papaya, so 'fruit' is a plain category label for it.

clue.text: Bear what is ridicule if repeated (4)

definitions.note: The second half defines the word only once it is said twice, which is the theme of the puzzle rather than a synonym of the answer.

blocks.note: the honey-loving bear of A A Milne's stories, and the one everybody thinks of first
said twice it becomes the verb for dismissing an idea as nonsense

explanation.surface: Putting up with something that turns into mockery the moment it is said again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like the verb, to put up with, and is the animal. The word doubled is a dismissive noise that British English has used for a couple of centuries.
explanation.definitionFit: Winnie-the-Pooh is the bear of A A Milne's stories, and to pooh-pooh a suggestion — the word repeated — is to ridicule it.

clue.text: Replacement notices changed as one result of twice dividing (10)

indicators.note: Something changed no longer looks the way it did, so these letters take up a different arrangement.

blocks.note: a sub is the replacement who comes off the bench
the seven letters of NOTICES, rearranged

explanation.surface: A stand-in rewriting the notices on the office board.
explanation.walkthrough: Divide something and you get sections; divide one of those again and you get what the definition describes. The prefix is also the bench player, which is how the two halves share a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Dividing produces sections, and dividing a section produces subsections, so the definition names the answer by how it came about.

clue.text: Cheat producing score in old notation (6-5)

definitions.note: The second half describes how the number twenty looks written down rather than giving a synonym, which is why 'producing' joins the halves instead of an equals sign.

blocks.note: to betray the person you were supposed to be in league with
a score is twenty, and twenty in Roman numerals is XX — a pair of the same character

explanation.surface: A cheat piling up points under some antique scoring system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score' is the trap: it wants to be points on a board, and it is the old word for twenty. Roman numerals are the 'old notation', and X hand-drawn is a saltire.
explanation.definitionFit: To double-cross someone is to cheat the partner who trusted you; and XX, the Roman twenty that a score means, is two crosses side by side.

clue.text: Nobel Laureate who lyrically discouraged doublethink (3,5)

definitions.text: Nobel Laureate who lyrically discouraged doublethink

blocks.note: read as one of the novelists or poets the literature prize usually goes to, and meant as the songwriter who took it in 2016
on the surface a writer warning against Orwell's doublethink; underneath, a lyric telling you not to think twice

explanation.surface: A Nobel winner warning the world in song against Orwellian doublethink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doublethink' is Orwell's word from Nineteen Eighty-Four and it sends you hunting for a novelist. The lyric wanted is 'Don't Think Twice, It's All Right', the 1963 B-side of 'Blowin' in the Wind'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nobel Prize in Literature went to this songwriter in 2016, and 'Don't Think Twice, It's All Right' is thinking twice discouraged in a lyric.

clue.text: New members of team reorganised Sing Sing (8)

indicators.note: Reorganised means put into a new arrangement, so these letters are re-set in a different order.

blocks.note: eight letters to work from, and a name that repeats itself like everything else here

explanation.surface: New arrivals shaking up the regime inside Sing Sing.
explanation.walkthrough: Sing Sing is the New York state prison on the Hudson, chosen because its name doubles. In British sport the word for players newly put under contract is the one wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A club's signings are the players it has just put under contract, so they are precisely a team's new members.

clue.text: Guardian etc. added section about double (6)

indicators.note: About means round the outside, so the added section closes over the piece named after it.

blocks.note: a PS, the postscript, is the section added at the end of a letter
an aper is one who apes another, copying them move for move

explanation.surface: A newspaper adding a supplement about somebody's lookalike.
explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian is one of Britain's national dailies, and 'etc.' is what widens a single title into the whole rack. 'Double' is the noun for a lookalike, and the -er ending turns aping into the man who does it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Guardian is a British national newspaper, and 'etc.' extends it from that one title to papers in general.

clue.text: Second person on computer is chasing kitty (6)

blocks.note: a mo is a moment — 'half a mo' — which is a second
whoever sits at the keyboard is the user

explanation.surface: The second person at the computer, off after the cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second person' reads as the grammarian's you, and 'computer' keeps that reading alive for a word longer. Mo for a moment is British shorthand, still heard in 'hang on a mo'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouser is a cat kept because it hunts mice, so the definition is a kitty caught in the act of chasing.

clue.text: Initially beat a retreat, then once more in German town (5-5)

blocks.note: the initial letter of BEAT
the article as it stands
a den is the room you retreat into
the instruction to do it again repeats the five letters just built

explanation.surface: Beating a retreat, then beating it again, all the way to Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat a retreat' is one phrase on the surface and three separate pieces underneath. The spa town's name is doubled to tell it apart from the other towns of its old German state.
explanation.definitionFit: Baden-Baden is the spa town in the Black Forest, so 'German town' names it by category.

clue.text: Reprimand making one sad or scared, losing head – it’s even worse in stereo? (6)

indicators.note: Losing its head means giving up the letter at the front, so the word starts one letter later than it did.

blocks.note: somebody in tears is tearful
somebody afraid is fearful, and the two words differ only in that first letter
the doubling joke — one in each ear at once — which contributes no letters

explanation.surface: A telling-off that leaves you miserable and frightened, and worse still through both speakers.
explanation.walkthrough: Sad and scared give two different words, and each loses its first letter to leave the same six. 'Head' invites the panicking sense and means nothing more than the front of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: An earful is a loud telling-off — 'she gave him an earful' — which is a reprimand in the same noun form.

clue.text: Silly ass – it follows direction repeatedly (6)

indicators.note: What follows something comes along behind it, so these two letters go after the compass point rather than in front.
Repeatedly means the same move is made again, so a second direction takes another pair of letters behind it.

blocks.note: n = north on the compass
the word as it stands
w = west, the second compass point the repeat calls for
and the same two letters again behind it

explanation.surface: A fool who keeps trailing along after whichever way he is pointed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direction' names no particular compass point, so the crossings decide which two are wanted. 'Silly ass' is Wodehouse-era British for a fool, ass meaning the donkey rather than the American word.
explanation.definitionFit: A nitwit is a fool, and 'silly ass' is the British public-school phrase for the same kind of person.

clue.text: Good argument for double, for example (4)

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
a row is a noisy quarrel

explanation.surface: A strong case for going double.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For example' works the reverse of its usual way round here: doubling is one instance of the answer rather than the answer being an instance of doubling. Row rhymes with cow when it means a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Doubling in size is one way of growing, and 'for example' flags that the definition is an instance of the wider verb.

clue.text: Reveal 13 (6)

definitions.note: The second definition is a cross-reference: the number stands for the answer at 13 across, which is a synonym of this one.

blocks.note: to let out what was meant to stay hidden, often without meaning to
the answer at 13 across, the verb for cheating the person who trusted you

explanation.walkthrough: The number is a cross-reference to 13 across, whose answer means the same as this one. The other half is the involuntary sense: a face gives away what its owner wanted kept quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: To betray a secret, or a nervous twitch, is to reveal it; and to betray an ally is to double-cross them, which is what 13 across spells out.

clue.text: With it in audition, one most like to make others double up (8)

definitions.text: most like to make others double up

indicators.note: In means inside, so the single letter it governs is planted in the middle of the word named beside it.

blocks.note: w = with, the standard shortening
the word as it stands
an audition is the test a performer sits
one = I, the Roman numeral, dropped in after the first letter

explanation.surface: At the audition, the most fashionable of them and the one best at getting a laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With it' reads as a single phrase meaning fashionable and is two separate pieces. 'Double up' is the laughing sense, bent over, which is how the definition joins the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: To double up is to bend over laughing, so whoever is likeliest to cause it is the wittiest in the room.

clue.text: Continent reflected about multinational group in hot spots (6)

indicators.note: About means round the outside, so the continent's letters end up on either side of what they enclose.

blocks.note: SA = South America
the United Nations, the body nearly every country belongs to
the same two letters mirrored, closing the far side

explanation.surface: A continent and its reflection surrounding an international gathering somewhere warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot spots' wants to be trouble abroad, and it is the wooden rooms you sit and sweat in. South America shortens to SA, and its mirror image is the puzzle's doubling in two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A sauna is a hot room you sit in to sweat, so 'hot spots' is a literal plural description of them rather than the trouble-abroad sense.

clue.text: Doppelgänger translated from writer in German (6)

indicators.note: Translated from a language means carried out of it, and here the answer is carried out of the words that follow, unbroken.

blocks.note: the letters sit unbroken across the three words: writeR IN GERman

explanation.surface: A German writer's word for a lookalike, brought over into English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In German' looks like an instruction to translate and is nothing of the kind — the language is never needed. Doppelgänger is literally 'double-goer', so the theme is in the clue's first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringer — as in a dead ringer — is somebody who looks exactly like another person, which is what a Doppelgänger is.
